title: Why MLLMs Struggle to Count: Overcoming Individuation and Aggregation Bottlenecks with ConvStack

paper.title: Why MLLMs Struggle to Count: Overcoming Individuation and Aggregation Bottlenecks with ConvStack
paper.abstract: Abstract Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual counting, especially as the number of objects increases. We study where these errors come from and identify two recurring bottlenecks. The first arises during object individuation: non-overlapping patchification can split a single object across multiple visual tokens, making it harder to form coherent object-level representations. The second appears during aggregation, where attention normalization can reduce the separation between representations of neighboring counts as numerosity grows. Based on these observations, we introduce ConvStack, a lightweight module that mixes local spatial information directly in the visual token space and injects the resulting features through zero-initialized residual connections. This design helps preserve local object structure while providing a more stable visual signal for downstream counting. Although ConvStack is trained only on counting data while updating about 0.5% of the model parameters, its gains extend beyond counting to broader spatial understanding, while general visual performance remains largely intact. Our mechanistic analysis shows that ConvStack improves the separation of counting representations and the encoding of spatial information within MLLMs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Scene understanding versus counting. Qwen3-VL-8B correctly describes the aerial display but counts seven airplanes instead of eight. ConvStack (ours) recovers the correct count. Modern Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Google DeepMind, 2024 ) inherit much of their visual capability from pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . While these encoders provide strong global representations that align well with language models, they remain surprisingly fragile on tasks requiring precise visual grounding. As shown in Figure 1 , an MLLM may accurately describe the semantic contents of an image while simultaneously failing to correctly answer how many objects are present ( Hasani et al., 2025 ; Che et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . We use visual counting as a minimal, highly revealing probe for this broader grounding deficit. Counting requires far more than merely detecting the presence of foreground semantics. A capable model must first parse raw patches into discrete, localized object units ( object individuation ) and then accumulate those units into a discrete numerosity ( counting aggregation ). In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis that identifies severe bottlenecks at both of these critical stages ( Section 3 ). First, we reveal an individuation bottleneck stemming from image patchification. Because standard Vision Transformers project nonoverlapping patches independently, they severely struggle to group fragmented geometric features across patch boundaries, making it difficult to form coherent representations of individual objects. Second, we identify an aggregation bottleneck driven by attention normalization. Even when objects are successfully individuated, they must still be aggregated by the network’s attention mechanisms. Under a homogeneous single-head model with fixed object and background representations, attention that favors objects yields progressively smaller signal increments between adjacent counts. This compression reduces the hidden state distances between neighboring counts and increases the sensitivity required for exact readout. These twin diagnostic insights naturally dictate our architectural solution: a robust counting model requires a local spatial prior to heal fragmented object boundaries, coupled with an additive signaling pathway that bypasses attention compression. Driven by this intuition, we propose ConvStack, a lightweight module that pairs localized convolutional feature extraction with deep residual fusion. By applying depthwise convolutions directly within the visual token space, ConvStack forces neighboring tokens to communicate, effectively bridging patch boundaries to construct clear, individuated object representations. To reinforce this visual evidence downstream, we inject the adapted features into the MLLM through residual connections. Zero-initialized adapter output projections preserve the input features at initialization. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions under which additive visual evidence supports stable count readout at the injection point. Through experiments ( Section 4 ), we evaluate how ConvStack affects counting, spatial understanding, and general visual performance. Remarkably, by fine tuning ConvStack exclusively on counting datasets, the model acquires substantial improvements not only in dense object counting but also across a wide range of broader spatial understanding benchmarks. The vision and language backbones remain frozen while the adapters and visual merger are trained. General visual performance remains broadly comparable, with gains on some benchmarks and decreases on others. In summary, this paper makes three primary contributions: • Mechanistic Diagnosis: Through theoretical analysis and synthetic diagnostics, we identify and formalize object individuation failure and counting aggregation collapse as two fundamental bottlenecks that systematically hinder the numeric and spatial reasoning capabilities of MLLMs. • Architectural Solution: We introduce ConvStack, a lightweight convolutional module that operates directly in the visual token space to explicitly aggregate and inject local geometric structures via residual connections. • Empirical Validation: We demonstrate that training ConvStack exclusively on counting tasks significantly boosts both dense counting in real images and broader spatial understanding in modern MLLMs (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B), with broadly comparable general visual performance.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Vision Transformers and convolutional bias. ViTs tokenize an image into nonoverlapping patches and rely on attention to mix spatial information ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) . This design provides global receptive fields but weakens early local inductive bias compared with CNNs ( LeCun et al., 1998 ) . Hybrid architectures reintroduce convolutional structure through convolutional attention projections, combinations of convolution and attention, and soft convolutional priors ( Wu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2021 ; d’Ascoli et al., 2021 ) . Early convolutions improve ViT optimization and visual recognition ( Xiao et al., 2021 ) , while Convpass demonstrates the value of convolutional inductive bias for adaptation with few trainable parameters ( Jie and Deng, 2022 ) . ConvStack shares this emphasis on local spatial processing and convolutional adaptation. We examine how these ideas support object individuation and count readout, combining local visual features with residual routes and drawing on DeepStack’s multilayer visual injection ( Meng et al., 2024 ) . Visual counting. Counting has long been treated as a problem of localizing countable evidence and aggregating it into a cardinality estimate. Classical counting methods and methods for crowd counting often estimate density maps or evidence about individual objects before summation ( Lempitsky and Zisserman, 2010 ) , while counting everyday objects emphasizes localization of individual instances and the difficulty of natural scenes ( Chattopadhyay et al., 2017 ) . Human enumeration also distinguishes small exact counts from larger approximate number judgments ( Kaufman et al., 1949 ; Trick and Pylyshyn, 1994 ; Feigenson et al., 2004 ) , motivating examination of how counting performance varies with numerosity. We use synthetic images to isolate whether an encoder forms object units under controlled changes in patch alignment, shape, color, and size, and examine performance on small versus large counts under balanced count frequencies. These experiments probe object individuation and count readout without assuming that a model implements human cognition or exhibits a universal subitizing boundary. Visual grounding in language models and shortcut diagnostics. Contrastive models such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and MLLMs such as LLaVA ( Liu et al., 2023 ) rely on visual encoders whose token representations are aligned to language. Spatial reasoning benchmarks and diagnostic datasets such as CLEVR ( Johnson et al., 2017 ) show that high overall VQA accuracy can coexist with shortcut behavior and weak compositional grounding. Our controlled results make the shortcut issue concrete: a model can appear to count perfectly when the data exposes a cue from the patch grid or object area. The proposed analysis therefore treats counting accuracy as meaningful only when the construction rules out such shortcuts and requires local object individuation.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We view visual counting as two complementary computations: object individuation , which forms distinct object representations, and information aggregation , which combines the resulting evidence to determine their number. We examine how local spatial features support object formation and how attention aggregates object evidence into a representation sensitive to count.

sections.heading: 3.1 Patchification Makes Object Individuation Harder
sections.text: ViTs learn large counts more slowly. To study counting under controlled conditions, we use SynDot and SynPoly, introduced by Che et al. (2026) . These datasets contain black disks and colored polygons, respectively, on white backgrounds, with 1 1 to 10 10 objects per image in our experiments. Figure 2: Local spatial features improve counting. Left: CNN learns faster than ViT on SynPoly. Right: ConvStack nearly closes the accuracy gap between small and large counts. The 1 × 1 1\times 1 route control leaves a substantial gap. We begin with a simple count classification task on SynPoly to examine how the visual encoder affects counting. We compare a standard ViT and a CNN, each with four layers, training both on SynPoly with balanced count frequencies and evaluating their frozen output embeddings at each epoch using a linear classification head. Under the same training protocol, the CNN reaches 99 % 99\% probe accuracy at epoch 16 16 , whereas the ViT reaches only 75.2 % 75.2\% by epoch 30 30 ( Figure 2 , left). The ViT achieves much lower accuracy for large counts than for small counts. In a separate three-seed comparison with balanced training counts, its mean accuracy is 97.7 % 97.7\% for counts 1 1 to 3 3 but 80.6 % 80.6\% for counts 4 4 to 10 10 . Moving the same disk changes the learning problem. We suspect that this difference stems from the ViT’s patchification of the input image. We next use SynDot to isolate patch geometry. These observations motivate introducing a local spatial prior into the visual encoder. Standard patch embedding projects each nonoverlapping patch independently, without combining information across patch boundaries. Shared, overlapping convolutional filters aggregate neighboring pixels and provide a natural way to introduce this prior ( Xiao et al., 2021 ; Jie and Deng, 2022 ) . For the controlled ViT experiments, we instantiate this idea with a convolutional branch operating on image pixels that extracts hierarchical local features and injects them into the ViT through residual connections ( Section B.4 ). To examine the role of learned spatial filtering, we compare ConvStack with a control that replaces each 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution with a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution, equivalent to a shared linear layer applied independently at each spatial location. This control retains the same depth, channel widths, pooling operations, and injection points. On SynPoly, ConvStack achieves 99.9 % 99.9\% mean accuracy across three seeds and reduces the accuracy gap between small and large counts from 17.0 17.0 to 0.1 0.1 percentage points. The 1 × 1 1\times 1 route control retains a gap of 12.9 12.9 percentage points ( Figure 2 , right). These results support learned spatial filtering as a useful inductive bias for visual counting. We next examine how this spatial prior affects count representations by comparing ViT, CNN, and ViT+ConvStack trained on SynPoly for 15 15 epochs with 500 500 images per count class. The t-SNE ( van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008 ) visualizations of their final image embeddings show substantial overlap among the ViT’s count classes, especially at larger counts ( Figure 4 ). These results show that local spatial filtering strengthens visual count representations, particularly at larger counts.

sections.heading: 3.3 The ConvStack Architecture
sections.text: Driven by the need to continuously inject stable counting evidence, we propose ConvStack, an architecture that pairs localized convolutional feature extraction with a deep residual fusion mechanism. To enhance the spatial reasoning capabilities of pretrained MLLMs, ConvStack operates directly in the visual token space ( Figure 6 ). Figure 6: Overview of ConvStack. Teal outlines highlight the ConvStack components. Variable names correspond to Equation 7 . At each adapter location, we reshape the visual tokens into a 2D grid X X and update it with a convolutional bottleneck: 𝒞 θ ​ ( X ) = W up ∗ GELU ⁡ ( K dw ∗ GELU ⁡ ( W down ∗ LN ⁡ ( X ) ) ) , X ~ = X + α ​ 𝒞 θ ​ ( X ) . \mathcal{C}_{\theta}(X)=W_{\mathrm{up}}*\operatorname{GELU}\left(K_{\mathrm{dw}}*\operatorname{GELU}(W_{\mathrm{down}}*\operatorname{LN}(X))\right),\qquad\widetilde{X}=X+\alpha\mathcal{C}_{\theta}(X). (7) Here, W down W_{\mathrm{down}} and W up W_{\mathrm{up}} are 1 × 1 1\times 1 projections that compress and restore the channel dimension, while the 3 × 3 3\times 3 depthwise convolution K dw K_{\mathrm{dw}} mixes neighboring tokens in the compressed space. A learnable scalar α \alpha scales the correction. The updated features X ~ \widetilde{X} are flattened into visual tokens for fusion with the hidden states at selected LLM layers. We initialize W up W_{\mathrm{up}} to zero so that each adapter starts as an identity mapping, preserving the pretrained features at initialization.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Data and baselines. We implement ConvStack on Qwen3-VL-8B ( Bai et al., 2025 ) and compare it with Spatial-MLLM-3B ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , LLaVA-SP Cropping-7B ( Lou et al., 2025 ) , and Honeybee-7B ( Cha et al., 2024 ) . We assess counting in real images on PixMo-Count ( Deitke et al., 2025 ) and CountBenchQA ( Beyer et al., 2024 ) . We evaluate spatial understanding on CV-Bench ( Tong et al., 2024 ) , SAT-real ( Ray et al., 2024 ) , SpatialEval ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and SAT-Spatial ( hunarbatra, 2025 ) . We assess general visual capability on POPE ( Li et al., 2023 ) , MME ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , MMBench-EN ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , MMMU ( Yue et al., 2024 ) , RealWorldQA ( xAI, 2024 ) , and MathVista ( Lu et al., 2024 ) . Evaluation uses deterministic decoding and each model’s image processor. Dataset descriptions, evaluation splits, and training variants are detailed in Appendix A . Training. Our standard training mixture combines examples from the PixMo-Count training split with 2,000 2{,}000 SynPoly and 2,000 2{,}000 SynDot examples, following the synthetic datasets introduced by Che et al. (2026) . For Qwen3-VL, we train convolutional adapters at vision layer 18 18 (ablation in Section C.1 ) and all native DeepStack levels, together with the visual merger. The remaining pretrained parameters are frozen. We train for one epoch with an effective batch size of 32 32 , a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , and loss on tokens in counting answers.

sections.text: Counting and Spatial Understanding. As shown in Table 2 , ConvStack-8B consistently outperforms both the base Qwen3-VL-8B and alternative spatial adapters. The most striking gains are in dense counting, where it achieves 75.19 % 75.19\% on PixMo-Count, an absolute improvement of 9.73 9.73 percentage points over the base model ( 65.46 % 65.46\% ). Furthermore, the injected local features systematically benefit broader spatial reasoning, establishing top scores on benchmarks like CV-Bench Spatial ( 93.20 % 93.20\% ) and SAT-Spatial ( 76.81 % 76.81\% ). Notably, ConvStack proves superior to existing workarounds like Pool SFE or Crop+DFI ( Lou et al., 2025 ) , and avoids the severe performance collapse caused by aggressive strategies for token reduction, such as C-Abstractor ( Cha et al., 2024 ) . sections.heading: 4.4 Mechanistic Analysis
sections.text: Internal representations of counting. To understand how ConvStack improves counting, we analyze its internal representations using 500 500 SynPoly images with object counts ranging from 1 1 to 10 10 . As shown in Figure 7 , ConvStack produces clearer clusters for each count, alongside an accuracy increase from 56.8 % 56.8\% to 98.8 % 98.8\% for counts 6 6 to 10 10 . In the original hidden space, mean cosine silhouette rises from 0.479 0.479 to 0.707 0.707 , and separation improves for every adjacent count pair ( Appendix D ). Figure 7: Counting accuracy and representations on SynPoly. (a) Accuracy by number class, with 50 50 images per class. (b,c) t-SNE of the final layer representation of the last prompt token for counts 1 1 to 10 10 . Probing spatial features via S-Space. To verify that these representation benefits extend beyond counting to general spatial grounding, we apply S-Space ( MirroS Team, 2026 ) to probe intermediate model representations on 500 500 MSCOCO images. S-Space allows us to linearly read out object coordinates (horizontal, vertical, and depth) directly from the hidden states. Figure 8 (a) highlights a representative failure of the base model, which incorrectly judges the dining table to be farther away than the refrigerator. ConvStack corrects this error, and looking at the internal S-Space readout ( Figure 8 (b)), we see the corresponding depth probe shift dramatically from − 0.28 -0.28 (incorrectly farther) to + 0.08 +0.08 (correctly closer). Zooming out to the full set of 500 500 images ( Figure 8 (c)), ConvStack yields consistent aggregate gains in representational accuracy across all three dimensions ( + 3.5 % +3.5\% horizontal, + 2.3 % +2.3\% vertical, and + 2.1 % +2.1\% depth). This confirms that explicitly mixing local visual features forces the network to maintain a much stronger internal grounding of physical object relations. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we identified two critical bottlenecks in the object individuation and counting aggregation processes that cause MLLMs to struggle with visual counting, especially for large numbers. To address these limitations, we proposed ConvStack, an architecture that effectively improves the separation of internal counting representations. Remarkably, by training exclusively on counting tasks, the model achieves significant improvements in both visual counting and broader spatial understanding. These gains are accompanied by broadly comparable general visual performance, supporting ConvStack as a practical approach to strengthening numeric and spatial reasoning in multimodal foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix A Datasets
sections.text: We describe the datasets used for training, counting diagnostics, and evaluation. The standard adaptation mixture uses the PixMo-Count training split and 2,000 examples each from SynPoly and SynDot.

sections.heading: A.1 Counting Data and Controlled Diagnostics
sections.text: PixMo-Count. PixMo-Count ( Deitke et al., 2025 ) contains natural images annotated with a target object category and its count, with point annotations provided for training. Its validation and test splits, verified by human annotators, cover counts from 2 to 10. We use examples from the training split for counting adaptation and evaluate accuracy for exact counts on the available test images. The current Qwen3 evaluation contains 524 test examples. SynPoly. SynPoly, introduced by Che et al. (2026) , contains colored polygons on a white background with variation in shape, size, color, and position. It tests counting under appearance variation while keeping the scene simple. We use 2,000 examples in the standard adaptation mixture. The controlled encoder experiments use balanced counts from 1 to 10 and resolutions chosen for each experiment. The counting suite for pretrained models additionally uses 380 generated test images at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, with 20 examples for each count from 1 to 19. The representation analysis in Figure 7 uses a separate set of 500 images, with 50 examples per count from 1 to 10. SynDot. SynDot, also introduced by Che et al. (2026) , contains black disks on a white background. Its simple appearance makes it useful for isolating the relationship between object placement and patch geometry. We use 2,000 examples in the standard adaptation mixture. For controlled diagnostics, we construct variants with objects at patch centers, at patch edges, or at random positions, with counts from 1 to 10. The counting suite for pretrained models uses 380 generated 512 × 512 512\times 512 test images covering counts from 1 to 19, with 20 examples per count. CountBenchQA. CountBenchQA ( Beyer et al., 2024 ) converts CountBench ( Paiss et al., 2023 ) into a visual question answering task by adding questions about object quantity. The original images contain between 2 and 10 instances of a target object. Our additional counting evaluations use the public test release of 491 images and accuracy for exact counts.

sections.heading: A.2 Spatial Understanding Benchmarks
sections.text: CV-Bench. CV-Bench ( Tong et al., 2024 ) recasts annotated images from ADE20K, COCO, and Omni3D as visual questions about counting, spatial relations, depth order, and relative distance. Our CV-Bench Spatial score averages accuracy equally over Relation (650 questions), Depth (600), and Distance (600), covering 1,850 questions. The counting category is excluded from this spatial score. SAT-real. SAT-real is the test split of Spatial Aptitude Training (SAT) that uses real images ( Ray et al., 2024 ) evaluating spatial relationships and changes involving objects or viewpoints, with one or two images per question. SpatialEval. SpatialEval ( Wang et al., 2024 ) evaluates spatial relationships, position, counting, and navigation through tasks involving maps, grids, mazes, and real images. Our experiments use a fixed subset of 150 visual questions with multiple choices shared across models and report answer accuracy on this subset. SAT-Spatial. We use the public SAT-Spatial-VQA release ( hunarbatra, 2025 ) , which contains 15,000 examples for spatial reasoning, each consisting of an image, a question, and an answer. Although the release names its split train , we use these examples only for evaluation. We retain the native questions and score normalized exact matches to the answer values.

sections.heading: A.3 General Visual Benchmarks
sections.text: POPE. POPE ( Li et al., 2023 ) measures object hallucination through yes/no questions about whether a specified object appears in an image. We use the random, popular, and adversarial subsets based on COCO, each containing 3,000 questions, and report F1 over all 9,000 questions. MME. MME ( Fu et al., 2026 ) evaluates perception and cognition across 14 tasks, including object recognition, spatial position, text recognition, and reasoning. Our evaluation contains 2,374 yes/no questions arranged in 1,187 pairs. Each task combines accuracy on individual questions with the accuracy of answering both questions in a pair correctly. We report the sum of perception and cognition scores. MMBench-EN. MMBench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) is a benchmark with multiple choices per question covering a broad range of visual perception and reasoning abilities. We use the cached English development set with 4,377 evaluation records and report accuracy using deterministic option extraction. MMMU. MMMU ( Yue et al., 2024 ) tests multimodal understanding and reasoning at an expert level across 30 academic subjects. We evaluate the validation split of 900 questions, which includes both questions with multiple choices and questions requiring free responses, and report accuracy with answer normalization for free responses. RealWorldQA. RealWorldQA ( xAI, 2024 ) evaluates understanding of everyday visual scenes, including photographs taken from vehicles. We use its test split of 765 examples, containing both questions with multiple choices and questions requiring short answers, and report accuracy after option extraction or answer normalization. MathVista. MathVista ( Lu et al., 2024 ) evaluates mathematical reasoning grounded in visual inputs such as diagrams, charts, and natural images. We use the testmini split of 1,000 examples and report accuracy with local answer extraction followed by normalization of answer types and numerical precision.

sections.heading: A.4 Images for Spatial Representation Analysis
sections.text: MSCOCO. MSCOCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) provides natural images of everyday scenes with annotations of object instances. We select 500 images for the S-Space analysis ( MirroS Team, 2026 ) in Section 4.4 , comparing horizontal, vertical, and depth information in the base model and its ConvStack adaptation. These images form a set for representation analysis.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.37096v1 [cs.CV] 29 Sep 2026 Why MLLMs Struggle to Count: Overcoming Individuation and Aggregation Bottlenecks with ConvStack Liwei Che Yihao Quan Sen Fang Hongyi Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Rutgers University Ranjay Krishna Ruixiang Tang Vladimir Pavlovic Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Rutgers University Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Washington Abstract Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual counting, especially as the number of objects increases. We study where these errors come from and identify two recurring bottlenecks. The first arises during object individuation: non-overlapping patchification can split a single object across multiple visual tokens, making it harder to form coherent object-level representations. The second appears during aggregation, where attention normalization can reduce the separation between representations of neighboring counts as numerosity grows. Based on these observations, we introduce ConvStack, a lightweight module that mixes local spatial information directly in the visual token space and injects the resulting features through zero-initialized residual connections. This design helps preserve local object structure while providing a more stable visual signal for downstream counting. Although ConvStack is trained only on counting data while updating about 0.5% of the model parameters, its gains extend beyond counting to broader spatial understanding, while general visual performance remains largely intact. Our mechanistic analysis shows that ConvStack improves the separation of counting representations and the encoding of spatial information within MLLMs. A Preprint Keywords Visual counting ⋅ \cdot Vision transformers ⋅ \cdot Spatial grounding ⋅ \cdot Multimodal large language models 1 Introduction Figure 1: Scene understanding versus counting. Qwen3-VL-8B correctly describes the aerial display but counts seven airplanes instead of eight. ConvStack (ours) recovers the correct count. Modern Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Google DeepMind, 2024 ) inherit much of their visual capability from pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . While these encoders provide strong global representations that align well with language models, they remain surprisingly fragile on tasks requiring precise visual grounding. As shown in Figure 1 , an MLLM may accurately describe the semantic contents of an image while simultaneously failing to correctly answer how many objects are present ( Hasani et al., 2025 ; Che et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . We use visual counting as a minimal, highly revealing probe for this broader grounding deficit. Counting requires far more than merely detecting the presence of foreground semantics. A capable model must first parse raw patches into discrete, localized object units ( object individuation ) and then accumulate those units into a discrete numerosity ( counting aggregation ). In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis that identifies severe bottlenecks at both of these critical stages ( Section 3 ). First, we reveal an individuation bottleneck stemming from image patchification. Because standard Vision Transformers project nonoverlapping patches independently, they severely struggle to group fragmented geometric features across patch boundaries, making it difficult to form coherent representations of individual objects. Second, we identify an aggregation bottleneck driven by attention normalization. Even when objects are successfully individuated, they must still be aggregated by the network’s attention mechanisms. Under a homogeneous single-head model with fixed object and background representations, attention that favors objects yields progressively smaller signal increments between adjacent counts. This compression reduces the hidden state distances between neighboring counts and increases the sensitivity required for exact readout. These twin diagnostic insights naturally dictate our architectural solution: a robust counting model requires a local spatial prior to heal fragmented object boundaries, coupled with an additive signaling pathway that bypasses attention compression. Driven by this intuition, we propose ConvStack, a lightweight module that pairs localized convolutional feature extraction with deep residual fusion. By applying depthwise convolutions directly within the visual token space, ConvStack forces neighboring tokens to communicate, effectively bridging patch boundaries to construct clear, individuated object representations. To reinforce this visual evidence downstream, we inject the adapted features into the MLLM through residual connections. Zero-initialized adapter output projections preserve the input features at initialization. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions under which additive visual evidence supports stable count readout at the injection point. Through experiments ( Section 4 ), we evaluate how ConvStack affects counting, spatial understanding, and general visual performance. Remarkably, by fine tuning ConvStack exclusively on counting datasets, the model acquires substantial improvements not only in dense object counting but also across a wide range of broader spatial understanding benchmarks. The vision and language backbones remain frozen while the adapters and visual merger are trained. General visual performance remains broadly comparable, with gains on some benchmarks and decreases on others. In summary, this paper makes three primary contributions: • Mechanistic Diagnosis: Through theoretical analysis and synthetic diagnostics, we identify and formalize object individuation failure and counting aggregation collapse as two fundamental bottlenecks that systematically hinder the numeric and spatial reasoning capabilities of MLLMs. • Architectural Solution: We introduce ConvStack, a lightweight convolutional module that operates directly in the visual token space to explicitly aggregate and inject local geometric structures via residual connections. • Empirical Validation: We demonstrate that training ConvStack exclusively on counting tasks significantly boosts both dense counting in real images and broader spatial understanding in modern MLLMs (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B), with broadly comparable general visual performance. 2 Related Work Vision Transformers and convolutional bias. ViTs tokenize an image into nonoverlapping patches and rely on attention to mix spatial information ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) . This design provides global receptive fields but weakens early local inductive bias compared with CNNs ( LeCun et al., 1998 ) . Hybrid architectures reintroduce convolutional structure through convolutional attention projections, combinations of convolution and attention, and soft convolutional priors ( Wu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2021 ; d’Ascoli et al., 2021 ) . Early convolutions improve ViT optimization and visual recognition ( Xiao et al., 2021 ) , while Convpass demonstrates the value of convolutional inductive bias for adaptation with few trainable parameters ( Jie and Deng, 2022 ) . ConvStack shares this emphasis on local spatial processing and convolutional adaptation. We examine how these ideas support object individuation and count readout, combining local visual features with residual routes and drawing on DeepStack’s multilayer visual injection ( Meng et al., 2024 ) . Visual counting. Counting has long been treated as a problem of localizing countable evidence and aggregating it into a cardinality estimate. Classical counting methods and methods for crowd counting often estimate density maps or evidence about individual objects before summation ( Lempitsky and Zisserman, 2010 ) , while counting everyday objects emphasizes localization of individual instances and the difficulty of natural scenes ( Chattopadhyay et al., 2017 ) . Human enumeration also distinguishes small exact counts from larger approximate number judgments ( Kaufman et al., 1949 ; Trick and Pylyshyn, 1994 ; Feigenson et al., 2004 ) , motivating examination of how counting performance varies with numerosity. We use synthetic images to isolate whether an encoder forms object units under controlled changes in patch alignment, shape, color, and size, and examine performance on small versus large counts under balanced count frequencies. These experiments probe object individuation and count readout without assuming that a model implements human cognition or exhibits a universal subitizing boundary. Visual grounding in language models and shortcut diagnostics. Contrastive models such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and MLLMs such as LLaVA ( Liu et al., 2023 ) rely on visual encoders whose token representations are aligned to language. Spatial reasoning benchmarks and diagnostic datasets such as CLEVR ( Johnson et al., 2017 ) show that high overall VQA accuracy can coexist with shortcut behavior and weak compositional grounding. Our controlled results make the shortcut issue concrete: a model can appear to count perfectly when the data exposes a cue from the patch grid or object area. The proposed analysis therefore treats counting accuracy as meaningful only when the construction rules out such shortcuts and requires local object individuation. 3 Method We view visual counting as two complementary computations: object individuation , which forms distinct object representations, and information aggregation , which combines the resulting evidence to determine their number. We examine how local spatial features support object formation and how attention aggregates object evidence into a representation sensitive to count. 3.1 Patchification Makes Object Individuation Harder ViTs learn large counts more slowly. We define visual counting as predicting n = | 𝒪 ⁡ ( x , q ) | n=|\mathcal{O}(x,q)| , where 𝒪 ⁡ ( x , q ) \mathcal{O}(x,q) denotes the set of objects in image x x specified by query q q . To study counting under controlled conditions, we use SynDot and SynPoly, introduced by Che et al. (2026) . These datasets contain black disks and colored polygons, respectively, on white backgrounds, with 1 1 to 10 10 objects per image in our experiments. Figure 2: Local spatial features improve counting. Left: CNN learns faster than ViT on SynPoly. Right: ConvStack nearly closes the accuracy gap between small and large counts. The 1 × 1 1\times 1 route control leaves a substantial gap. We begin with a simple count classification task on SynPoly to examine how the visual encoder affects counting. We compare a standard ViT and a CNN, each with four layers, training both on SynPoly with balanced count frequencies and evaluating their frozen output embeddings at each epoch using a linear classification head. Under the same training protocol, the CNN reaches 99 % 99\% probe accuracy at epoch 16 16 , whereas the ViT reaches only 75.2 % 75.2\% by epoch 30 30 ( Figure 2 , left). The ViT achieves much lower accuracy for large counts than for small counts. In a separate three-seed comparison with balanced training counts, its mean accuracy is 97.7 % 97.7\% for counts 1 1 to 3 3 but 80.6 % 80.6\% for counts 4 4 to 10 10 . Moving the same disk changes the learning problem. We suspect that this difference stems from the ViT’s patchification of the input image. We next use SynDot to isolate patch geometry. A ViT divides an image x ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 x\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} into M = H ​ W / p 2 M=HW/p^{2} nonoverlapping patches of size p × p p\times p . The fraction of that object assigned to each patch is ρ k ​ i = | S k ∩ P i | | S k | , ∑ i = 1 M ρ k ​ i = 1 . \rho_{ki}=\frac{|S_{k}\cap P_{i}|}{|S_{k}|},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{M}\rho_{ki}=1. At a patch center , one token contains the entire disk: max i ⁡ ρ k ​ i = 1 \max_{i}\rho_{ki}=1 . At a shared edge , two tokens contain equal halves: ρ k ​ i = ρ k ​ j = 1 / 2 \rho_{ki}=\rho_{kj}=1/2 . With random placement , splits are generally asymmetric. The chosen sizes of disks and patches often leave a dominant fragment in one token. The displayed center, random, and edge runs first reach 100 % 100\% probe accuracy in every class at epochs 1 1 , 9 9 , and 14 14 , respectively, and all finish at 100 % 100\% . When each disk lies within a distinct patch, the object count equals the number of occupied patches. Splitting disks across patch boundaries breaks this direct correspondence and distributes object evidence across multiple tokens. Figure 3: Patch geometry changes learning speed. Numbers indicate the first epoch with 100 % 100\% accuracy across all count classes. Overlapping filters provide a local prior. These observations motivate introducing a local spatial prior into the visual encoder. Standard patch embedding projects each nonoverlapping patch independently, without combining information across patch boundaries. Shared, overlapping convolutional filters aggregate neighboring pixels and provide a natural way to introduce this prior ( Xiao et al., 2021 ; Jie and Deng, 2022 ) . For the controlled ViT experiments, we instantiate this idea with a convolutional branch operating on image pixels that extracts hierarchical local features and injects them into the ViT through residual connections ( Section B.4 ). To examine the role of learned spatial filtering, we compare ConvStack with a control that replaces each 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution with a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution, equivalent to a shared linear layer applied independently at each spatial location. This control retains the same depth, channel widths, pooling operations, and injection points. On SynPoly, ConvStack achieves 99.9 % 99.9\% mean accuracy across three seeds and reduces the accuracy gap between small and large counts from 17.0 17.0 to 0.1 0.1 percentage points. The 1 × 1 1\times 1 route control retains a gap of 12.9 12.9 percentage points ( Figure 2 , right). These results support learned spatial filtering as a useful inductive bias for visual counting. This observation motivates us to investigate how attention aggregation ( Che et al., 2026 ) preserves distinctions between counts. The contribution of an additional object. To isolate aggregation from individuation, consider n n objects each contained in a distinct patch: ρ k ​ i ∈ { 0 , 1 } \rho_{ki}\in\{0,1\} for all k = 1 , … , n k=1,\ldots,n and i = 1 , … , M i=1,\ldots,M , with no patch containing more than one object. Assuming one visual token per patch at the LLM input, the number of object tokens is then N = n N=n . To address these limitations, we proposed ConvStack, an architecture that effectively improves the separation of internal counting representations. Remarkably, by training exclusively on counting tasks, the model achieves significant improvements in both visual counting and broader spatial understanding. These gains are accompanied by broadly comparable general visual performance, supporting ConvStack as a practical approach to strengthening numeric and spatial reasoning in multimodal foundation models.
